### qb-0001 · Customer list

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — One table, three named columns, no filter. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** SELECT columns (`basics.select`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables customers · read-only
- **Objective:** Select named columns from one table.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 0 (Meet your first SELECT)

**Task.** Return customer_id, country and region for every Retail customer.

**Return:** `customer_id`, `country`, `region` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 848 rows on the visible data):

| customer_id | country | region |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 12347 | Iceland | Europe |
| 12353 | Bahrain | Rest of World |
| 12359 | Cyprus | Europe |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT customer_id, country, region FROM customers
```

**Why it works.** SELECT chooses columns; every customer row is returned once.

**Hints:** (1) List the three columns after SELECT. (2) No WHERE clause is needed.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Returns every column instead of the three requested.

### qb-0002 · Weather stations in the West

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — A single numeric comparison on one table. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** WHERE (`filtering.where`)
- **Dataset:** Weather · tables stations · read-only
- **Objective:** Filter rows with a numeric comparison.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 3 (Filter with WHERE), 4 (Comparisons & ranges)

**Task.** Return station_id, station_name and longitude for every station west of 100°W (longitude below −100).

**Return:** `station_id`, `station_name`, `longitude` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 30 rows on the visible data):

| station_id | station_name | longitude |
| --- | --- | --- |
| USW00003131 | San Diego Montgomery Fld | -117.1375 |
| USW00003184 | Phoenix Deer Valley Muni Airport | -112.0661 |
| USW00022521 | Honolulu International Airport | -157.9394 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT station_id, station_name, longitude FROM stations WHERE longitude < -100
```

**Why it works.** Longitude decreases going west, so stations west of 100°W have longitude below −100.

**Hints:** (1) Western longitudes are negative numbers. (2) WHERE longitude < -100.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Selects the eastern stations.

### qb-0003 · Kitchen catalog from most to least expensive

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — Filter one category and sort with a tie-breaker. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** ORDER BY (`basics.order-by`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables products · read-only
- **Objective:** Sort results deterministically.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 8 (Sort & limit)

**Task.** Return stock_code, description and list_price for products in category 3 (Kitchen & Dining) that have a list price, most expensive first; break ties by stock_code.

**Return:** `stock_code`, `description`, `list_price` · row order is checked

**Example output** (first 3 of 570 rows on the visible data):

| stock_code | description | list_price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22656 | VINTAGE BLUE KITCHEN CABINET | 295 |
| 22655 | VINTAGE RED KITCHEN CABINET | 125 |
| 21764 | VINTAGE WOODEN PLATE RACK | 39.95 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT stock_code, description, list_price FROM products WHERE category_id = 3 AND list_price IS NOT NULL ORDER BY list_price DESC, stock_code
```

**Why it works.** DESC puts the highest prices first; stock_code decides the order among equal prices.

**Hints:** (1) Filter category_id = 3 AND list_price IS NOT NULL. (2) ORDER BY list_price DESC, stock_code.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Sorts from cheapest to most expensive.

### qb-0004 · Appointments that produced no visit

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — One IS NULL test. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** NULL handling (`filtering.null`)
- **Dataset:** Healthcare · tables appointments · read-only
- **Objective:** Find missing values with IS NULL.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 7 (Understand NULL)

**Task.** Return appointment_id, patient_id and status for every appointment that has no linked encounter.

**Return:** `appointment_id`, `patient_id`, `status` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 2510 rows on the visible data):

| appointment_id | patient_id | status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | cancelled |
| 8 | 1 | cancelled |
| 26 | 5 | cancelled |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT appointment_id, patient_id, status FROM appointments WHERE encounter_id IS NULL
```

**Why it works.** Cancelled, missed and future appointments have no encounter; IS NULL finds them.

**Hints:** (1) The link is encounter_id. (2) Use IS NULL, not = NULL.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- = NULL is never true, so no rows are returned.

### qb-0005 · The three cheapest products

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — Filter, sort and LIMIT with a tie-breaker. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** LIMIT (`basics.limit`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables products · read-only
- **Objective:** Keep the first n rows of a defined order.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 8 (Sort & limit)

**Task.** Return stock_code, description and list_price for the three cheapest merchandise products (is_merchandise = 1) with a positive list price, cheapest first; break ties by stock_code.

**Return:** `stock_code`, `description`, `list_price` · row order is checked

**Example output** (first 3 of 3 rows on the visible data):

| stock_code | description | list_price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PADS | PADS TO MATCH ALL CUSHIONS | 0.001 |
| 16045 | POPART WOODEN PENCILS ASST | 0.04 |
| 17061 | ASSORTED SHAPED STENCIL FOR HENNA | 0.04 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT stock_code, description, list_price FROM products WHERE is_merchandise = 1 AND list_price > 0 ORDER BY list_price, stock_code LIMIT 3
```

**Why it works.** Sorting ascending and keeping three rows returns the cheapest; the tie-breaker makes the choice stable.

**Hints:** (1) Filter is_merchandise = 1 AND list_price > 0. (2) ORDER BY list_price, stock_code LIMIT 3.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Includes non-merchandise codes.

### qb-0006 · Rename and convert a column

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — Aliases and one arithmetic expression. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** Column aliases (`basics.alias`)
- **Dataset:** U.S. Flights · tables routes · read-only
- **Objective:** Name output columns and calculated values.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 1 (Aliases & calculated columns)

**Task.** For every route that departs from JFK, return route_id, destination, miles (the distance_miles column) and km (miles × 1.609344, rounded to the nearest whole number).

**Return:** `route_id`, `destination`, `miles`, `km` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 55 rows on the visible data):

| route_id | destination | miles | km |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2512 | ATL | 760 | 1223 |
| 2513 | AUS | 1521 | 2448 |
| 2514 | BNA | 765 | 1231 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT route_id, destination, distance_miles AS miles, ROUND(distance_miles * 1.609344) AS km FROM routes WHERE origin = 'JFK'
```

**Why it works.** AS names a column or an expression in the result.

**Hints:** (1) distance_miles AS miles. (2) ROUND(distance_miles * 1.609344) AS km.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Columns are not named miles and km.

### qb-0007 · Borough and service-zone combinations

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — DISTINCT over two columns. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** DISTINCT (`basics.distinct`)
- **Dataset:** Mobility · tables zones · read-only
- **Objective:** Return each distinct combination once.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 2 (Unique values with DISTINCT)

**Task.** Return each distinct pair of borough_id and service_zone found in zones.

**Return:** `borough_id`, `service_zone` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 10 rows on the visible data):

| borough_id | service_zone |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | EWR |
| 2 | Boro Zone |
| 3 | Boro Zone |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT borough_id, service_zone FROM zones
```

**Why it works.** DISTINCT removes duplicate (borough_id, service_zone) rows.

**Hints:** (1) SELECT DISTINCT borough_id, service_zone. (2) DISTINCT applies to the whole row.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Returns one row per zone, with duplicates.

### qb-0008 · Developers who joined during 2024

- **Difficulty:** Warm-up — A half-open timestamp range. (rubric: Warm-up, score 0)
- **Topic:** BETWEEN & ranges (`filtering.between`)
- **Dataset:** Developer Platform · tables developers · read-only
- **Objective:** Filter a whole year without boundary errors.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 4 (Comparisons & ranges)

**Task.** Return developer_id, username and joined_at for developers who joined during calendar year 2024.

**Return:** `developer_id`, `username`, `joined_at` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 864 rows on the visible data):

| developer_id | username | joined_at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | dreyes10 | 2024-03-30 21:30:35 |
| 11 | dcooper11 | 2024-05-21 15:39:45 |
| 13 | tmehta13 | 2024-05-30 06:26:19 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT developer_id, username, joined_at FROM developers WHERE joined_at >= '2024-01-01' AND joined_at < '2025-01-01'
```

**Why it works.** The half-open range includes all of 31 December and nothing from 2025.

**Hints:** (1) joined_at is a timestamp. (2) joined_at >= '2024-01-01' AND joined_at < '2025-01-01'.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Misses people who joined later on 31 December.

### qb-0009 · Orders by year and type

- **Difficulty:** Easy — GROUP BY two expressions. (rubric: Easy, score 2)
- **Topic:** GROUP BY (`aggregation.group-by`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders · read-only
- **Objective:** Count rows per group.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 10 (Group into summaries)

**Task.** Return year (YYYY of ordered_at), order_type and orders: the number of orders for each year and order type.

**Return:** `year`, `order_type`, `orders` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 6 rows on the visible data):

| year | order_type | orders |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2009 | cancellation | 56 |
| 2009 | sale | 257 |
| 2010 | cancellation | 492 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT substr(ordered_at, 1, 4) AS year, order_type, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY year, order_type
```

**Why it works.** Grouping by both values gives one row per year and type.

**Hints:** (1) substr(ordered_at, 1, 4) AS year. (2) GROUP BY year, order_type.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Groups by type only, so the year is arbitrary.

### qb-0010 · Providers with no encounters

- **Difficulty:** Easy — An anti-join with LEFT JOIN or NOT EXISTS. (rubric: Easy, score 1.5)
- **Topic:** Missing relationships / anti-joins (`joins.anti`)
- **Dataset:** Healthcare · tables providers, encounters · read-only
- **Objective:** Find rows with no related rows.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 15 (Keep unmatched rows), 18 (Ask whether a row exists)

**Task.** Return provider_id, full_name and specialty for every provider who has no encounters.

**Return:** `provider_id`, `full_name`, `specialty` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 29 rows on the visible data):

| provider_id | full_name | specialty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 115 | Mark Ahmed | Orthopedics |
| 137 | Lucia Robinson | Cardiology |
| 178 | Nia Abbott | Orthopedics |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT p.provider_id, p.full_name, p.specialty FROM providers p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM encounters e WHERE e.provider_id = p.provider_id)
```

**Why it works.** An anti-join keeps left rows with no matching right rows.

**Hints:** (1) LEFT JOIN encounters and keep rows where the encounter side is NULL. (2) Or use NOT EXISTS.

**Equivalent solutions tested:** 1.

**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Returns providers who do have encounters.

### qb-0011 · Frequent customers

- **Difficulty:** Easy — GROUP BY with a HAVING filter on a count. (rubric: Easy, score 2.5)
- **Topic:** HAVING (`aggregation.having`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders · read-only
- **Objective:** Filter groups after aggregation.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 11 (Filter groups with HAVING)

**Task.** Return customer_id and sale_orders for identified customers with at least 20 sale orders.

**Return:** `customer_id`, `sale_orders` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 36 rows on the visible data):

| customer_id | sale_orders |
| --- | --- |
| 12431 | 27 |
| 12569 | 32 |
| 12980 | 21 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS sale_orders FROM orders WHERE order_type = 'sale' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20
```

**Why it works.** WHERE chooses sale orders; HAVING keeps customers whose count reaches 20.

**Hints:** (1) WHERE order_type = 'sale' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL. (2) HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Counts cancellations as orders.

### qb-0012 · 2011 net sales by department

- **Difficulty:** Easy — Four-table join and one grouped measure. (rubric: Medium, score 3.5)
- **Topic:** GROUP BY (`aggregation.group-by`); tags `joins.multi`
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items, products, categories · read-only
- **Objective:** Aggregate a line-level measure at a coarser grain.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 16 (Revenue across tables)

**Task.** Return department and net_sales (quantity × unit_price over all 2011 order lines, sales and cancellations, rounded to 2) for each product department.

**Return:** `department`, `net_sales` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 9 rows on the visible data):

| department | net_sales |
| --- | --- |
| Fashion | 117937.1 |
| Gifts | 213158.33 |
| Home | 650126.53 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT c.department, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS net_sales FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN products p ON p.stock_code = i.stock_code JOIN categories c ON c.category_id = p.category_id WHERE o.ordered_at >= '2011-01-01' AND o.ordered_at < '2012-01-01' GROUP BY c.department
```

**Why it works.** Each line joins to exactly one order, product and category, so summing after the joins is safe.

**Hints:** (1) Join order_items → orders (date), → products → categories (department). (2) Filter ordered_at to 2011 with a half-open range.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**

- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables invitations · read-only
- **Objective:** Group on a normalized text key.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 11 (Filter groups with HAVING), 33 (Clean strings & cast values)

**Task.** Return email (lower-cased, trimmed invitee_email) and workspaces: the number of different workspaces that invited it, for emails invited by more than one workspace.

| --- | --- |
| aaron.kaur@mail.example | 2 |
| alex.shah@mail.example | 2 |
| amara.chang@mail.example | 2 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(invitee_email)) AS email, COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) AS workspaces FROM invitations GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(invitee_email)) HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) > 1
```

**Why it works.** Normalizing the email makes equal addresses group together; distinct workspaces are what the question counts.

- **Objective:** Average a measure per group.

**Task.** For 2025 regular-season games, return venue_name and avg_attendance (rounded to 0 decimals) per ballpark. Games without recorded attendance are ignored by the average.


- **Dataset:** Retail · tables products · read-only
- **Objective:** Classify values into bands.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 12 (Make decisions with CASE)

**Task.** For merchandise products, return stock_code, list_price and band: 'unpriced' when list_price is NULL, 'budget' below 1, 'standard' below 5, otherwise 'premium'.

| 15060A | NULL | unpriced |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT stock_code, list_price, CASE WHEN list_price IS NULL THEN 'unpriced' WHEN list_price < 1 THEN 'budget' WHEN list_price < 5 THEN 'standard' ELSE 'premium' END AS band FROM products WHERE is_merchandise = 1
```

### qb-0022 · How long did delivery take?

- **Difficulty:** Easy — Join, earliest delivered scan and a day difference. (rubric: Medium, score 3)
- **Topic:** Date differences (`dates.diff`)
- **Dataset:** Logistics · tables shipments, packages, tracking_events · read-only
- **Objective:** Measure the time between two events.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 26 (Dates & monthly analysis), 39 (Date boundaries & monthly buckets)

**Task.** For packages in shipments created in February 2025 that have a delivered scan, return package_id and days_to_deliver: days from the shipment’s created_at to the package’s first delivered scan, rounded to 1 decimal.

**Return:** `package_id`, `days_to_deliver` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 2676 rows on the visible data):

| package_id | days_to_deliver |
| --- | --- |
| 18 | 4.1 |
| 21 | 2.1 |
| 22 | 4.6 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT p.package_id, ROUND(julianday(MIN(e.event_at)) - julianday(s.created_at), 1) AS days_to_deliver FROM shipments s JOIN packages p ON p.shipment_id = s.shipment_id JOIN tracking_events e ON e.package_id = p.package_id AND e.event_type = 'delivered' WHERE s.created_at >= '2025-02-01' AND s.created_at < '2025-03-01' GROUP BY p.package_id, s.created_at
```

**Why it works.** The first delivered scan ends the journey; duplicates or later scans do not change MIN.

**Hints:** (1) MIN(event_at) of delivered events per package. (2) julianday(delivered) − julianday(created_at).



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Uses the last delivered scan, inflating delivery time when scans repeat.

### qb-0023 · Create a wishlist table

**Task.** Create wishlist with customer_id INTEGER referencing customers(customer_id), stock_code TEXT referencing products(stock_code), added_at TEXT NOT NULL, and PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, stock_code). Insert (12347, '85123A', '2011-12-01') and (12347, '22423', '2011-12-02'). Return customer_id, stock_code and added_at.

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE TABLE wishlist (customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(customer_id), stock_code TEXT REFERENCES products(stock_code), added_at TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, stock_code)); INSERT INTO wishlist VALUES (12347, '85123A', '2011-12-01'), (12347, '22423', '2011-12-02'); SELECT customer_id, stock_code, added_at FROM wishlist
```

### qb-0025 · Big spenders for their state

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Per-customer totals compared with a correlated per-state average. (rubric: Medium, score 5.25)
- **Topic:** Correlated subqueries (`subqueries.correlated`); tags `subqueries.cte`
- **Dataset:** Finance / Payments · tables customers, accounts, cards, authorizations, settlements · read-only
- **Objective:** Compare each row with an average of its own group.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 17 (Subqueries)

**Task.** Using settled card amounts, return customer_id, state and settled_cents for customers whose total settled card spend is above the average total of customers in the same state (only customers with any settled spend count toward that average).

**Return:** `customer_id`, `state`, `settled_cents` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 355 rows on the visible data):

| customer_id | state | settled_cents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | AZ | 131000 |
| 4 | IL | 715055 |
| 11 | NC | 184149 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH totals AS (SELECT c.customer_id, c.state, SUM(s.amount_cents) AS settled_cents FROM settlements s JOIN authorizations a ON a.authorization_id = s.authorization_id JOIN cards k ON k.card_id = a.card_id JOIN accounts x ON x.account_id = k.account_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = x.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.state) SELECT t.customer_id, t.state, t.settled_cents FROM totals t WHERE t.settled_cents > (SELECT AVG(t2.settled_cents) FROM totals t2 WHERE t2.state = t.state)
```

**Why it works.** The correlated subquery recomputes the state average for each customer’s state.

**Hints:** (1) First total settlements per customer in a CTE. (2) Compare with (SELECT AVG(settled_cents) FROM totals t2 WHERE t2.state = t.state).



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Compares with the national average instead of the state’s.

### qb-0026 · Monthly sales after cancellations

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Conditional sums at month grain. (rubric: Medium, score 4.5)
- **Topic:** Revenue & order value (`analytics.revenue`); tags `aggregation.conditional`
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items · read-only
- **Objective:** Separate gross sales from cancellations and net them.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 13 (Conditional aggregation), 16 (Revenue across tables)

**Task.** For 2011, return month (YYYY-MM), gross_sales (lines on sale orders), cancellations (lines on cancellation orders, as a negative amount) and net_sales, each rounded to 2.

**Return:** `month`, `gross_sales`, `cancellations`, `net_sales` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 12 rows on the visible data):

| month | gross_sales | cancellations | net_sales |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2011-01 | 51803.5 | -3070.01 | 48733.49 |
| 2011-02 | 75745.9 | -6353.18 | 69392.72 |
| 2011-03 | 81117.99 | -2422.9 | 78695.09 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT substr(o.ordered_at, 1, 7) AS month, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_type = 'sale' THEN i.quantity * i.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS gross_sales, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_type = 'cancellation' THEN i.quantity * i.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS cancellations, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS net_sales FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.ordered_at >= '2011-01-01' AND o.ordered_at < '2012-01-01' GROUP BY month
```

**Why it works.** Cancellation lines carry negative quantities, so net = gross + cancellations.

**Hints:** (1) SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_type = 'sale' THEN i.quantity * i.unit_price ELSE 0 END). (2) Net is the sum of all lines.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Net ignores cancellations.

### qb-0027 · Bestsellers within each category

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Aggregate, rank within partitions, keep ties. (rubric: Hard, score 7)
- **Topic:** RANK / DENSE_RANK (`windows.rank`); tags `windows.top-n`
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items, products · read-only
- **Objective:** Rank within groups and keep the top N including ties.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 22 (RANK & DENSE_RANK), 53 (Top N per group & ties)

**Task.** For sale lines in 2011, return category_id, stock_code and units for each category’s top three products by units sold, including ties (use RANK).

**Return:** `category_id`, `stock_code`, `units` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 49 rows on the visible data):

| category_id | stock_code | units |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 22952 | 1708 |
| 1 | 22086 | 1275 |
| 1 | 22910 | 1054 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT category_id, stock_code, units FROM (SELECT p.category_id, i.stock_code, SUM(i.quantity) AS units, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category_id ORDER BY SUM(i.quantity) DESC) AS r FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN products p ON p.stock_code = i.stock_code WHERE o.order_type = 'sale' AND o.ordered_at >= '2011-01-01' AND o.ordered_at < '2012-01-01' AND p.category_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY p.category_id, i.stock_code) WHERE r <= 3
```

**Why it works.** RANK keeps every product tied at third place.

**Hints:** (1) Sum quantity per category and product first. (2) RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY units DESC) <= 3.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- ROW_NUMBER drops products tied at third place.

### qb-0029 · More pull requests than their manager

**Task.** Return developer_id, prs, manager_id and manager_prs for developers who authored more pull requests than their manager. Developers and managers with no pull requests count as 0.

```sql
WITH c AS (SELECT d.developer_id, d.manager_id, COUNT(p.pull_request_id) AS prs FROM developers d LEFT JOIN pull_requests p ON p.author_id = d.developer_id GROUP BY d.developer_id, d.manager_id) SELECT e.developer_id, e.prs, e.manager_id, m.prs AS manager_prs FROM c e JOIN c m ON m.developer_id = e.manager_id WHERE e.prs > m.prs
```

### qb-0030 · Days with no orders

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Generate a date series and anti-join it. (rubric: Hard, score 6.75)
- **Topic:** Date series & missing days (`dates.series`); tags `subqueries.recursive`, `joins.anti`
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders · read-only
- **Objective:** Find gaps by comparing with a complete calendar.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 27 (Recursive CTEs), 35 (CROSS JOIN & a complete date grid)

**Task.** Return day for every calendar day in 2011 on which no order of any type was placed.

**Return:** `day` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 83 rows on the visible data):

| day |
| --- |
| 2011-01-01 |
| 2011-01-02 |
| 2011-01-03 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (SELECT '2011-01-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2011-12-31') SELECT day FROM days WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.ordered_at >= days.day AND o.ordered_at < date(days.day, '+1 day'))
```

**Why it works.** The series supplies every day; the anti-join keeps the empty ones (mostly Saturdays and holidays).

**Hints:** (1) WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (SELECT '2011-01-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2011-12-31'). (2) Keep days with no order whose date(ordered_at) equals the day.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Lists days that had orders; empty days cannot come from the orders table.

### qb-0031 · First and latest order per customer

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Two ROW_NUMBER rankings or MIN/MAX with a join back. (rubric: Hard, score 7)
- **Topic:** ROW_NUMBER (`windows.row-number`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders · read-only
- **Objective:** Pick the first and last row per group.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 21 (Window functions: ROW_NUMBER), 25 (Latest row per group)

**Task.** For identified customers, return customer_id, first_invoice (invoice_no of the earliest sale order), latest_invoice (invoice_no of the latest sale order) and sale_orders. Break timestamp ties by order_id.

**Return:** `customer_id`, `first_invoice`, `latest_invoice`, `sale_orders` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 841 rows on the visible data):

| customer_id | first_invoice | latest_invoice | sale_orders |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12347 | 529924 | 581180 | 8 |
| 12353 | 529304 | 553900 | 2 |
| 12359 | 490382 | 571034 | 10 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT customer_id, MAX(CASE WHEN rn_first = 1 THEN invoice_no END) AS first_invoice, MAX(CASE WHEN rn_last = 1 THEN invoice_no END) AS latest_invoice, COUNT(*) AS sale_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, invoice_no, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, order_id) AS rn_first, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn_last FROM orders WHERE order_type = 'sale' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL) GROUP BY customer_id
```

**Why it works.** Two orderings identify the first and last order without a second scan.

**Hints:** (1) ROW_NUMBER() ascending and descending in one subquery. (2) Group by customer and pick each rank-1 invoice with MAX(CASE …).



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Invoice numbers are not guaranteed to follow time order.

### qb-0032 · Orders whose payments don’t match

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Pre-aggregate two child tables to avoid fan-out. (rubric: Hard, score 8)
- **Topic:** Join fan-out & cardinality (`joins.fan-out`); tags `warehousing.reconciliation`
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items, payments · read-only
- **Objective:** Join independent children at the parent grain.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 49 (Multi-grain joins without fan-out), 50 (Revenue & payment reconciliation)

**Task.** For sale orders placed in November 2011, return order_id, order_total (sum of quantity × unit_price, rounded to 2) and captured (sum of captured payments, rounded to 2, 0 when none) for orders whose captured amount differs from the order total.

**Return:** `order_id`, `order_total`, `captured` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 12 rows on the visible data):

| order_id | order_total | captured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6154 | 296.76 | 0 |
| 6169 | 300.1 | 0 |
| 6183 | 213.08 | 0 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH t AS (SELECT o.order_id, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS order_total FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_type = 'sale' AND o.ordered_at >= '2011-11-01' AND o.ordered_at < '2011-12-01' GROUP BY o.order_id), p AS (SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS captured FROM payments WHERE status = 'captured' GROUP BY order_id) SELECT t.order_id, t.order_total, COALESCE(p.captured, 0) AS captured FROM t LEFT JOIN p ON p.order_id = t.order_id WHERE COALESCE(p.captured, 0) <> t.order_total
```

**Why it works.** Each side is reduced to one row per order before joining, so split payments do not multiply line amounts.

**Hints:** (1) Aggregate lines per order and captured payments per order separately. (2) Compare the rounded values.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Joining lines and payments together multiplies both sums.

### qb-0033 · Flight outcomes by origin state

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Conditional counts with a ratio per group. (rubric: Easy, score 2.5)
- **Topic:** Conditional aggregation (`aggregation.conditional`)
- **Dataset:** U.S. Flights · tables flights, airports · read-only
- **Objective:** Count several categories side by side.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 13 (Conditional aggregation), 32 (Ratios, ROUND & NULLIF)

**Task.** Return state, flights, cancelled, diverted and cancelled_pct (0–100, 2 decimals) per origin airport state.

**Return:** `state`, `flights`, `cancelled`, `diverted`, `cancelled_pct` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 52 rows on the visible data):

| state | flights | cancelled | diverted | cancelled_pct |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AK | 811 | 17 | 5 | 2.1 |
| AL | 622 | 26 | 1 | 4.18 |
| AR | 506 | 13 | 0 | 2.57 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT a.state, COUNT(*) AS flights, SUM(f.cancelled) AS cancelled, SUM(f.diverted) AS diverted, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(f.cancelled) / COUNT(*), 2) AS cancelled_pct FROM flights f JOIN airports a ON a.airport_code = f.origin GROUP BY a.state
```

**Why it works.** Flag columns sum to counts; the percentage uses all scheduled flights as its denominator.

**Hints:** (1) JOIN airports a ON a.airport_code = f.origin. (2) SUM(cancelled) works because cancelled is 0 or 1.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Integer division truncates the percentage.

### qb-0034 · Loyal customers who never returned anything

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Combine a HAVING count with NOT EXISTS. (rubric: Medium, score 4)
- **Topic:** IN / EXISTS / NOT EXISTS (`subqueries.exists`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders · read-only
- **Objective:** Combine positive and negative existence tests.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 18 (Ask whether a row exists), 31 (NOT IN and the NULL trap)

**Task.** Return customer_id and sale_orders for identified customers with at least 10 sale orders who never had a cancellation order.

**Return:** `customer_id`, `sale_orders` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 14 rows on the visible data):

| customer_id | sale_orders |
| --- | --- |
| 12599 | 13 |
| 12913 | 13 |
| 13291 | 11 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS sale_orders FROM orders o WHERE o.order_type = 'sale' AND o.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND c.order_type = 'cancellation') GROUP BY o.customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10
```

**Why it works.** NOT EXISTS removes customers with any cancellation before counting.

**Hints:** (1) Group sale orders per customer with HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10. (2) NOT EXISTS a cancellation for the same customer.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- NOT IN with anonymous (NULL) cancellations returns no rows.

### qb-0035 · Average order value by month

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Aggregate lines to orders, then orders to months. (rubric: Medium, score 4.75)
- **Topic:** Revenue & order value (`analytics.revenue`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items · read-only
- **Objective:** Average at the right grain.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 20 (Readable queries with CTEs), 16 (Revenue across tables)

**Task.** For sale orders in 2011, return month and avg_order_value: the average of order totals (sum of quantity × unit_price per order), rounded to 2.

**Return:** `month`, `avg_order_value` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 12 rows on the visible data):

| month | avg_order_value |
| --- | --- |
| 2011-01 | 343.07 |
| 2011-02 | 498.33 |
| 2011-03 | 382.63 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH t AS (SELECT o.order_id, substr(o.ordered_at, 1, 7) AS month, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_type = 'sale' AND o.ordered_at >= '2011-01-01' AND o.ordered_at < '2012-01-01' GROUP BY o.order_id, month) SELECT month, ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order_value FROM t GROUP BY month
```

**Why it works.** Averaging line amounts would give the average line value, not the average order.

**Hints:** (1) First total each order in a CTE. (2) Then AVG(order_total) per month.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**

### qb-0036 · Deployments versus incidents

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Two independent aggregates joined at organization grain. (rubric: Hard, score 8)
- **Topic:** GROUP BY (`aggregation.group-by`); tags `joins.fan-out`
- **Dataset:** Developer Platform · tables organizations, repositories, deployments, incidents · read-only
- **Objective:** Compare two measures from different tables per group.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 16 (Revenue across tables), 49 (Multi-grain joins without fan-out)

**Task.** For every organization, return organization_id, production_deploys (production deployments of its repositories), failed_deploys (those with status failed or rolled_back) and incidents (incidents on its repositories), using 0 when none.

**Return:** `organization_id`, `production_deploys`, `failed_deploys`, `incidents` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 60 rows on the visible data):

| organization_id | production_deploys | failed_deploys | incidents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 82 | 10 | 6 |
| 2 | 196 | 23 | 19 |
| 3 | 58 | 5 | 3 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH d AS (SELECT r.organization_id, COUNT(*) AS production_deploys, SUM(dp.status IN ('failed', 'rolled_back')) AS failed_deploys FROM deployments dp JOIN repositories r ON r.repository_id = dp.repository_id WHERE dp.environment = 'production' GROUP BY r.organization_id), i AS (SELECT r.organization_id, COUNT(*) AS incidents FROM incidents x JOIN repositories r ON r.repository_id = x.repository_id GROUP BY r.organization_id) SELECT o.organization_id, COALESCE(d.production_deploys, 0) AS production_deploys, COALESCE(d.failed_deploys, 0) AS failed_deploys, COALESCE(i.incidents, 0) AS incidents FROM organizations o LEFT JOIN d ON d.organization_id = o.organization_id LEFT JOIN i ON i.organization_id = o.organization_id
```

**Why it works.** Each measure is summarized separately so deployments do not multiply incidents.

**Hints:** (1) Aggregate deployments and incidents per organization separately. (2) LEFT JOIN both aggregates to organizations.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Joining deployments and incidents together multiplies both counts.

### qb-0037 · Keep one invitation per person

- **Difficulty:** Medium — ROW_NUMBER over a normalized key with a tie-breaker. (rubric: Medium, score 4)
- **Topic:** Deduplication (`cleaning.dedupe`)
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables invitations · read-only
- **Objective:** Keep the first record per duplicate key.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 44 (Deduplicate event retries)

**Task.** Keep one invitation per invitee email (lower-cased and trimmed): the earliest sent_at, ties broken by the lowest invitation_id. Return invitation_id, email and sent_at.

**Return:** `invitation_id`, `email`, `sent_at` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 6412 rows on the visible data):

| invitation_id | email | sent_at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4363 | aaliyah.anderson@evergreensecurity2101.example | 2025-03-31 06:44:03 |
| 2265 | aaliyah.anderson@summitcapital1064.example | 2024-11-24 21:41:28 |
| 3725 | aaliyah.baker@bluesecurity1783.example | 2025-02-11 13:18:16 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT invitation_id, email, sent_at FROM (SELECT invitation_id, LOWER(TRIM(invitee_email)) AS email, sent_at, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(invitee_email)) ORDER BY sent_at, invitation_id) AS rn FROM invitations) WHERE rn = 1
```

**Why it works.** Partitioning by the normalized email treats repeated invitations of one person as duplicates.

**Hints:** (1) ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(invitee_email)) ORDER BY sent_at, invitation_id). (2) Keep rn = 1.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- The smallest id and the earliest time can come from different invitations.

### qb-0038 · A covering index for unit totals

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Index design verified by the plan. (rubric: Easy, score 2)
- **Topic:** Indexes (`optimization.indexes`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables order_items · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Answer a query from an index alone.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 66 (Indexes: observe a real access path)

**Task.** Create an index that lets SQLite answer total units per stock code from the index alone (stock_code, then quantity). Then return stock_code and units (sum of quantity) for stock codes beginning with '2272'.

**Return:** `stock_code`, `units` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 9 rows on the visible data):

| stock_code | units |
| --- | --- |
| 22720 | 877 |
| 22721 | 64 |
| 22722 | 615 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_items_code_qty ON order_items(stock_code, quantity); SELECT stock_code, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM order_items WHERE stock_code >= '2272' AND stock_code < '2273' GROUP BY stock_code
```

**Why it works.** With both columns in the index, SQLite never reads the table rows.

**Hints:** (1) CREATE INDEX … ON order_items(stock_code, quantity). (2) The plan should show USING COVERING INDEX.

**Plan contract:** `{"indexes":[{"id":"cover","table":"order_items","columns":["stock_code","quantity"]}],"access":[{"index":"cover","strategy":"covering-search"}]}`

**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**

### qb-0039 · A reusable customer totals view

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Create a view and query it. (rubric: Hard, score 7)
- **Topic:** Views, temp tables & triggers (`engineering.views`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Define a reusable query object.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 62 (Views: reusable query definitions)

**Task.** Create view customer_totals with customer_id, orders (distinct sale orders) and net_sales (all lines, rounded to 2) for identified customers. Return the 10 customers with the highest net_sales from the view, highest first (ties by customer_id).

**Return:** `customer_id`, `orders`, `net_sales` · row order is checked

**Example output** (first 3 of 10 rows on the visible data):

| customer_id | orders | net_sales |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 18102 | 145 | 570380.61 |
| 14298 | 82 | 90489.31 |
| 15838 | 34 | 72727.41 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE VIEW customer_totals AS SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_type = 'sale' THEN o.order_id END) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS net_sales FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY o.customer_id; SELECT customer_id, orders, net_sales FROM customer_totals ORDER BY net_sales DESC, customer_id LIMIT 10
```

**Why it works.** The view stores the definition; ordering and limiting happen in the query that reads it.

**Hints:** (1) CREATE VIEW customer_totals AS SELECT … (2) Then SELECT … FROM customer_totals ORDER BY net_sales DESC, customer_id LIMIT 10.



**Object checks:** 1 (state/catalog check)

**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Returns the rows but never creates the view.

### qb-0040 · Second-highest home-run total per team

- **Objective:** Find the second distinct value within each group.

**Task.** For the 2025 regular season, return team_id, player_id and home_runs for players at the second-highest distinct home-run total on their team (all ties).

| ANA | wardt002 | 36 |
| ARI | carrc005 | 31 |
| ATH | langs001 | 31 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT team_id, player_id, home_runs FROM (SELECT s.team_id, s.player_id, SUM(s.home_runs) AS home_runs, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY s.team_id ORDER BY SUM(s.home_runs) DESC) AS dr FROM player_game_stats s JOIN games g ON g.game_id = s.game_id WHERE g.game_type = 'regular' GROUP BY s.team_id, s.player_id) WHERE dr = 2
```

**Why it works.** DENSE_RANK gives every player sharing the second distinct total rank 2.

### qb-0041 · Next-month retention by signup cohort

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Cohort assignment, a relative period and a mature-cohort rule. (rubric: Medium, score 5.75)
- **Topic:** Cohorts & retention (`analytics.retention`); tags `dates.buckets`
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables users, events · read-only
- **Objective:** Measure the share of a cohort active in the following month.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 47 (Cohorts & exact-day retention)

**Task.** For users created from January to May 2025, return cohort_month (YYYY-MM of created_at), cohort_size (users in the cohort), retained (users with any event in the calendar month after their cohort month) and retention_pct (0–100, 2 decimals).

**Rules.**
- Use occurred_at for activity.
- June 2025 is the last complete month, so the May cohort is the newest mature cohort.

**Return:** `cohort_month`, `cohort_size`, `retained`, `retention_pct` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 5 rows on the visible data):

| cohort_month | cohort_size | retained | retention_pct |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2025-01 | 919 | 384 | 41.78 |
| 2025-02 | 863 | 377 | 43.68 |
| 2025-03 | 1086 | 431 | 39.69 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH c AS (SELECT user_id, substr(created_at, 1, 7) AS cohort_month, date(created_at, 'start of month', '+1 month') AS next_start FROM users WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-06-01') SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size, SUM(kept) AS retained, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(kept) / COUNT(*), 2) AS retention_pct FROM (SELECT c.cohort_month, EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM events e WHERE e.user_id = c.user_id AND e.occurred_at >= c.next_start AND e.occurred_at < date(c.next_start, '+1 month')) AS kept FROM c) GROUP BY cohort_month
```

**Why it works.** Each user is counted once in their cohort; retention asks about one specific later month.

**Hints:** (1) The next month starts at date(created_at, 'start of month', '+1 month'). (2) EXISTS an event in [next month start, the month after).



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Counts activity in any later month, not the next month.

### qb-0042 · Longest winning streak

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Gaps and islands over game results per team. (rubric: Hard, score 9)
- **Topic:** Gaps & islands (`windows.gaps-islands`); tags `windows.row-number`
- **Dataset:** Sports · tables games · read-only
- **Objective:** Find the longest run of consecutive wins.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 21 (Window functions: ROW_NUMBER), 24 (Compare rows with LAG)

**Task.** For the 2025 regular season, return team_id and longest_streak: each team’s longest run of consecutive wins, ordering its games by game_date then game_number.

**Rules.**
- Each game counts for both teams; a win means scoring more runs than the opponent.

**Return:** `team_id`, `longest_streak` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 30 rows on the visible data):

| team_id | longest_streak |
| --- | --- |
| ANA | 8 |
| ARI | 5 |
| ATH | 5 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH tg AS (SELECT home_team_id AS team_id, game_date, game_number, home_score > away_score AS won FROM games WHERE season = 2025 AND game_type = 'regular' UNION ALL SELECT away_team_id, game_date, game_number, away_score > home_score FROM games WHERE season = 2025 AND game_type = 'regular'), seq AS (SELECT team_id, won, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY game_date, game_number) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team_id, won ORDER BY game_date, game_number) AS grp FROM tg) SELECT team_id, MAX(n) AS longest_streak FROM (SELECT team_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS n FROM seq WHERE won = 1 GROUP BY team_id, grp) GROUP BY team_id
```

**Why it works.** Inside a streak both row numbers advance together, so their difference identifies the island.

**Hints:** (1) Unpivot games into one row per team and game. (2) Within each team, ROW_NUMBER over all games minus ROW_NUMBER over wins is constant inside a streak.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Counts all wins, not consecutive wins.

### qb-0043 · Customer segment at order time

- **Difficulty:** Hard — An as-of join to half-open history intervals. (rubric: Easy, score 2.5)

- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, customer_history · read-only
- **Objective:** Attribute each event to the version valid at its time.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 83 (Latest-state reporting versus SCD Type 2)

**Task.** For sale orders placed in November 2011 by identified customers, return order_id, customer_id and segment: the customer’s segment in the customer_history version valid on the order date.

| order_id | customer_id | segment |

| 6139 | 17733 | occasional |
| 6140 | 17389 | key_account |
| 6141 | 17166 | occasional |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, h.segment FROM orders o JOIN customer_history h ON h.customer_id = o.customer_id AND h.valid_from <= date(o.ordered_at) AND (h.valid_to IS NULL OR date(o.ordered_at) < h.valid_to) WHERE o.order_type = 'sale' AND o.ordered_at >= '2011-11-01' AND o.ordered_at < '2011-12-01'
```

**Why it works.** Exactly one version contains each date, so each order keeps its grain.

**Hints:** (1) Join on customer_id and date(ordered_at) within [valid_from, valid_to). (2) valid_to is NULL for the current version.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Uses today’s segment rather than the one valid in November.

### qb-0044 · Overlapping prescription fills

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Self-join with an interval-overlap condition and pair ordering. (rubric: Easy, score 2)
- **Topic:** Validation & types (`cleaning.validation`); tags `joins.self`
- **Dataset:** Healthcare · tables medications · read-only
- **Objective:** Detect overlapping intervals within a group.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 34 (Self-joins & referral relationships), 78 (Product validity with LEAD & half-open intervals)

**Task.** For patients 1–300, return patient_id, medication_name, first_id and second_id for every pair of fills of the same drug for the same patient whose supply intervals overlap. Intervals are [start_date, stop_date); list each pair once with first_id < second_id.

**Return:** `patient_id`, `medication_name`, `first_id`, `second_id` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 441 rows on the visible data):

| patient_id | medication_name | first_id | second_id |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Metformin 500 mg tablet | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | Albuterol 90 mcg inhaler | 6 | 7 |
| 2 | Albuterol 90 mcg inhaler | 7 | 8 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT a.patient_id, a.medication_name, a.medication_id AS first_id, b.medication_id AS second_id FROM medications a JOIN medications b ON b.patient_id = a.patient_id AND b.medication_name = a.medication_name AND a.medication_id < b.medication_id AND a.start_date < b.stop_date AND b.start_date < a.stop_date WHERE a.patient_id BETWEEN 1 AND 300
```

**Why it works.** The two-sided comparison catches every overlap, including one interval inside another.

**Hints:** (1) Two half-open intervals overlap when a.start < b.stop AND b.start < a.stop. (2) a.medication_id < b.medication_id lists each pair once.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Treats fills that only touch at the stop date as overlapping.

### qb-0045 · Management chain for every developer

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Recursive walk upward, building a path string. (rubric: Hard, score 7.25)
- **Topic:** Recursive CTEs (`subqueries.recursive`)
- **Dataset:** Developer Platform · tables developers · read-only
- **Objective:** Follow a hierarchy and accumulate the path.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 27 (Recursive CTEs)

**Task.** For organization 5, return developer_id and chain: the developer’s id followed by each manager’s id up to the top, separated by ' > ' (for example '512 > 498 > 480').

**Return:** `developer_id`, `chain` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 14 rows on the visible data):

| developer_id | chain |
| --- | --- |
| 389 | 389 |
| 390 | 390 > 389 |
| 391 | 391 > 390 > 389 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE walk(developer_id, current_id, chain) AS (SELECT developer_id, manager_id, CAST(developer_id AS TEXT) FROM developers WHERE organization_id = 5 UNION ALL SELECT w.developer_id, d.manager_id, w.chain || ' > ' || d.developer_id FROM walk w JOIN developers d ON d.developer_id = w.current_id) SELECT developer_id, chain FROM walk WHERE current_id IS NULL
```

**Why it works.** Each step moves to the manager; the walk ends at the person with no manager.

**Hints:** (1) Start at every developer with path = their own id. (2) Repeatedly join to the current manager and append its id; keep the row whose last node has no manager.

- Shows only the direct manager and leaves the top person with a NULL chain.

### qb-0046 · Median home attendance per team

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Median with even and odd counts using window positions. (rubric: Medium, score 5.5)
- **Topic:** Medians, shares & ratios (`analytics.statistics`)
- **Dataset:** Sports · tables games · read-only
- **Objective:** Compute a median without a built-in function.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 21 (Window functions: ROW_NUMBER), 53 (Top N per group & ties)

**Task.** For 2025 regular-season home games with recorded attendance, return team_id and median_attendance per home team. With an even count, average the two middle values.

**Return:** `team_id`, `median_attendance` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 30 rows on the visible data):

| team_id | median_attendance |
| --- | --- |
| ANA | 30609 |
| ARI | 29252 |
| ATH | 9185 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT home_team_id AS team_id, AVG(attendance) AS median_attendance FROM (SELECT home_team_id, attendance, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY home_team_id ORDER BY attendance, game_id) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY home_team_id) AS n FROM games WHERE season = 2025 AND game_type = 'regular' AND attendance IS NOT NULL) WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2) GROUP BY home_team_id
```

**Why it works.** For odd n both positions are the same row; for even n they are the two middle rows.

**Hints:** (1) ROW_NUMBER() ascending and COUNT(*) OVER per team. (2) Keep positions (n + 1) / 2 and (n + 2) / 2 with integer division, then AVG.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Returns the mean, not the median.

### qb-0047 · Build a country history from invoices

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Collapse consecutive equal values into intervals. (rubric: Hard, score 14)
- **Topic:** History, SCD & as-of (`warehousing.history`); tags `windows.gaps-islands`
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders · read-only
- **Objective:** Turn event snapshots into validity intervals.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 78 (Product validity with LEAD & half-open intervals), 24 (Compare rows with LAG)

**Task.** For identified customers whose invoices list more than one country, return customer_id, country, valid_from and valid_to: one row per run of consecutive invoices (by ordered_at, order_id) with the same country. valid_from is the run’s first invoice date; valid_to is the next run’s first invoice date, NULL for the last run.

**Return:** `customer_id`, `country`, `valid_from`, `valid_to` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 13 rows on the visible data):

| customer_id | country | valid_from | valid_to |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12431 | Belgium | 2010-01-15 | 2010-03-04 |
| 12431 | Australia | 2010-03-04 | 2010-07-19 |
| 12431 | Belgium | 2010-07-19 | 2010-08-17 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH multi AS (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT country) > 1), marked AS (SELECT o.customer_id, o.country, date(o.ordered_at) AS d, o.ordered_at, o.order_id, CASE WHEN LAG(o.country) OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.ordered_at, o.order_id) = o.country THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_run FROM orders o JOIN multi USING (customer_id)), runs AS (SELECT customer_id, country, d, SUM(new_run) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, order_id) AS run FROM marked), starts AS (SELECT customer_id, run, country, MIN(d) AS valid_from FROM runs GROUP BY customer_id, run, country) SELECT customer_id, country, valid_from, LEAD(valid_from) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY run) AS valid_to FROM starts
```

**Why it works.** A run starts whenever the country changes; consecutive runs then give half-open intervals.

**Hints:** (1) Mark a new run when the country differs from the previous invoice’s country (LAG). (2) Running SUM of the marks numbers the runs; then LEAD the run start.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Merges non-consecutive runs of the same country into one overlapping interval.

### qb-0048 · Settlements, refunds and disputes

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Three sources at one grain, then a precedence of statuses. (rubric: Hard, score 7.5)
- **Topic:** Reconciliation & quality gates (`warehousing.reconciliation`); tags `joins.fan-out`
- **Dataset:** Finance / Payments · tables settlements, refunds, chargebacks · read-only
- **Objective:** Reconcile one amount against two kinds of recovery.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 49 (Multi-grain joins without fan-out), 50 (Revenue & payment reconciliation)

**Task.** For settlements in Q1 2025 with any refund or credited chargeback, return settlement_id, settled_cents, refunded_cents, disputed_cents (credited chargebacks) and status: 'double_recovery' when refunds plus credited disputes exceed the settlement, 'fully_recovered' when they equal it, otherwise 'partially_recovered'.

**Return:** `settlement_id`, `settled_cents`, `refunded_cents`, `disputed_cents`, `status` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 523 rows on the visible data):

| settlement_id | settled_cents | refunded_cents | disputed_cents | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 18689 | 4372 | 4372 | 0 | fully_recovered |
| 7857 | 899 | 271 | 0 | partially_recovered |
| 34657 | 2499 | 0 | 2499 | fully_recovered |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH r AS (SELECT settlement_id, SUM(amount_cents) AS cents FROM refunds GROUP BY settlement_id), c AS (SELECT settlement_id, SUM(amount_cents) AS cents FROM chargebacks WHERE status = 'credited' GROUP BY settlement_id) SELECT s.settlement_id, s.amount_cents AS settled_cents, COALESCE(r.cents, 0) AS refunded_cents, COALESCE(c.cents, 0) AS disputed_cents, CASE WHEN COALESCE(r.cents, 0) + COALESCE(c.cents, 0) > s.amount_cents THEN 'double_recovery' WHEN COALESCE(r.cents, 0) + COALESCE(c.cents, 0) = s.amount_cents THEN 'fully_recovered' ELSE 'partially_recovered' END AS status FROM settlements s LEFT JOIN r ON r.settlement_id = s.settlement_id LEFT JOIN c ON c.settlement_id = s.settlement_id WHERE s.settled_at >= '2025-01-01' AND s.settled_at < '2025-04-01' AND (r.cents IS NOT NULL OR c.cents IS NOT NULL)
```

**Why it works.** Summarizing each source first keeps multiple refunds from multiplying the dispute amount.

**Hints:** (1) Aggregate refunds and credited chargebacks per settlement separately. (2) COALESCE missing sums to 0 before comparing.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Joining refunds and disputes together multiplies their sums.

### qb-0049 · Design a flight lookup index

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Composite index column order verified by the plan. (rubric: Easy, score 0.5)
- **Topic:** Indexes (`optimization.indexes`)
- **Dataset:** U.S. Flights · tables flights · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Choose index columns that match a lookup.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 66 (Indexes: observe a real access path), 67 (SARGable ranges, not speed commandments)

**Task.** Create an index that lets SQLite search flights by destination and flight date together, then return flight_id, origin and scheduled_departure for flights arriving at SEA on 2025-02-14.

**Return:** `flight_id`, `origin`, `scheduled_departure` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 37 rows on the visible data):

| flight_id | origin | scheduled_departure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 57001 | FAI | 2025-02-14 01:46 |
| 57005 | PSC | 2025-02-14 05:00 |
| 57006 | EUG | 2025-02-14 05:00 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_flights_dest_date ON flights(destination, flight_date); SELECT flight_id, origin, scheduled_departure FROM flights WHERE destination = 'SEA' AND flight_date = '2025-02-14'
```

**Why it works.** Both filter columns are equality conditions, so a two-column index finds the rows directly.

**Hints:** (1) Put the equality columns in the index: destination, flight_date. (2) Check the plan for SEARCH flights USING INDEX.

**Plan contract:** `{"indexes":[{"id":"lookup","table":"flights","columns":["destination","flight_date"]}],"access":[{"index":"lookup","strategy":"search"}]}`

**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- The index does not cover the filter columns.

### qb-0050 · Cover the export query

- **Difficulty:** Hard — A covering index that serves filter and output columns. (rubric: Easy, score 0.5)
- **Topic:** Indexes (`optimization.indexes`)
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables events · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Serve a query entirely from an index.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 66 (Indexes: observe a real access path)

**Task.** Create an index so this export is answered from the index alone, then run it: user_id and occurred_at for data_exported events in May 2025.

**Return:** `user_id`, `occurred_at` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 592 rows on the visible data):

| user_id | occurred_at |
| --- | --- |
| 7747 | 2025-05-01 01:38:15 |
| 8397 | 2025-05-01 02:42:24 |
| 6140 | 2025-05-01 02:53:21 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_events_export ON events(event_name, occurred_at, user_id); SELECT user_id, occurred_at FROM events WHERE event_name = 'data_exported' AND occurred_at >= '2025-05-01' AND occurred_at < '2025-06-01'
```

**Why it works.** The equality column leads, the range follows, and the output column completes the covering index.

**Hints:** (1) Index (event_name, occurred_at, user_id). (2) The plan should say COVERING INDEX.

**Plan contract:** `{"indexes":[{"id":"export","table":"events","columns":["event_name","occurred_at","user_id"]}],"access":[{"index":"export","strategy":"covering-search"}]}`

### qb-0051 · Make the event-day filter searchable

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Rewrite a function-wrapped predicate as a range. (rubric: Easy, score 0.5)
- **Topic:** Query plans & SARGable filters (`optimization.plans`)
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables events · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Keep an indexed column bare in the filter.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 67 (SARGable ranges, not speed commandments)

**Task.** Create an index on events(occurred_at). Rewrite the filter date(occurred_at) = '2025-06-15' so the index can be searched, and return delivery_id and event_name for that day.

**Return:** `delivery_id`, `event_name` · any row order

| delivery_id | event_name |
| --- | --- |
| 127204 | invite_sent |
| 127205 | subscription_canceled |
| 127206 | report_shared |

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_events_time ON events(occurred_at); SELECT delivery_id, event_name FROM events WHERE occurred_at >= '2025-06-15' AND occurred_at < '2025-06-16'
```

### qb-0052 · Latest failed deliveries without a sort

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Index order that satisfies ORDER BY … LIMIT. (rubric: Easy, score 0.5)
- **Topic:** Query plans & SARGable filters (`optimization.plans`)
- **Dataset:** Logistics · tables tracking_events · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Use index order to avoid a temporary sort.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 66 (Indexes: observe a real access path)

**Task.** Create an index so the 20 most recent delivery_failed scans can be read in order without a temporary sort, then return event_id, package_id and event_at for them, newest first.

**Return:** `event_id`, `package_id`, `event_at` · row order is checked

**Example output** (first 3 of 20 rows on the visible data):

| event_id | package_id | event_at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 100484 | 3327 | 2025-04-30 23:00:00 |
| 100455 | 1699 | 2025-04-30 21:16:00 |
| 100439 | 197 | 2025-04-30 20:43:00 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_events_type_time ON tracking_events(event_type, event_at); SELECT event_id, package_id, event_at FROM tracking_events WHERE event_type = 'delivery_failed' ORDER BY event_at DESC LIMIT 20
```

**Why it works.** Within one event_type the index is already ordered by event_at.

**Hints:** (1) Index (event_type, event_at). (2) ORDER BY event_at DESC LIMIT 20 can walk the index backwards.

### qb-0053 · An ordered upgrade funnel

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Three ordered steps at workspace grain with time windows. (rubric: Hard, score 8.25)
- **Topic:** Funnels & conversion (`analytics.conversion`)
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables events · read-only
- **Objective:** Count workspaces completing steps in order.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 46 (Ordered conversion funnels)

**Task.** For workspaces with a pricing_viewed event in 2025, return one row with viewed, checked_out and subscribed: workspaces whose first 2025 pricing view is followed (at or after) by a checkout_started, and that checkout followed within 24 hours by subscription_started.

**Rules.**
- Use the earliest qualifying event for each step after the previous step.

**Return:** `viewed`, `checked_out`, `subscribed` · any row order

**Example output** (first 1 of 1 rows on the visible data):

| viewed | checked_out | subscribed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 837 | 666 | 554 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH v AS (SELECT account_id, MIN(occurred_at) AS t1 FROM events WHERE event_name = 'pricing_viewed' AND occurred_at >= '2025-01-01' GROUP BY account_id), c AS (SELECT v.account_id, MIN(e.occurred_at) AS t2 FROM v JOIN events e ON e.account_id = v.account_id AND e.event_name = 'checkout_started' AND e.occurred_at >= v.t1 GROUP BY v.account_id), s AS (SELECT c.account_id FROM c JOIN events e ON e.account_id = c.account_id AND e.event_name = 'subscription_started' AND e.occurred_at >= c.t2 AND e.occurred_at < datetime(c.t2, '+1 day') GROUP BY c.account_id) SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM v) AS viewed, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM c) AS checked_out, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s) AS subscribed
```

**Why it works.** Each step is anchored to the time of the step before it.

**Hints:** (1) MIN(occurred_at) per account for each step, constrained by the previous step’s time. (2) Count accounts in each CTE.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Ignores order and includes sales-led upgrades without a checkout.

### qb-0054 · Abandoned checkouts

- **Difficulty:** Medium — NOT EXISTS with a time window after each event. (rubric: Medium, score 5.5)
- **Topic:** Funnels & conversion (`analytics.conversion`); tags `subqueries.exists`
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables events · read-only
- **Objective:** Find events not followed by an outcome.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 18 (Ask whether a row exists), 46 (Ordered conversion funnels)

**Task.** Return event_id, account_id and occurred_at for logical checkout_started events (one per event_id) with no subscription_started for the same workspace within 24 hours after the checkout.

**Return:** `event_id`, `account_id`, `occurred_at` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 183 rows on the visible data):

| event_id | account_id | occurred_at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| evt_0000332 | 6 | 2024-04-21 00:46:01 |
| evt_0000588 | 11 | 2024-02-21 08:57:03 |
| evt_0001014 | 15 | 2024-03-31 04:50:14 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT c.event_id, c.account_id, c.occurred_at FROM (SELECT * FROM (SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY received_at, delivery_id) AS copy FROM events e WHERE event_name = 'checkout_started') WHERE copy = 1) c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM events s WHERE s.account_id = c.account_id AND s.event_name = 'subscription_started' AND s.occurred_at >= c.occurred_at AND s.occurred_at < datetime(c.occurred_at, '+1 day'))
```

**Why it works.** The anti-join keeps checkouts with no subscription in the window; retried checkouts are counted once.

**Hints:** (1) Deduplicate by event_id first. (2) NOT EXISTS a subscription_started in [occurred_at, occurred_at + 1 day).



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Returns retried checkouts twice.

### qb-0055 · Audit duplicate scans

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Group by the identity of a scan and measure the spread. (rubric: Hard, score 7.25)
- **Topic:** Deduplication (`cleaning.dedupe`)
- **Dataset:** Logistics · tables tracking_events · read-only
- **Objective:** Profile duplicates before removing them.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 44 (Deduplicate event retries)

**Task.** For scanner events, return package_id, event_type, warehouse_id, copies and spread_minutes (minutes between the first and last copy, rounded to 0 decimals) for every package, event type and warehouse scanned more than once within 15 minutes of its first scan.

**Rules.**
- Copies are scanner events with the same package_id, event_type and warehouse_id whose event_at is within 15 minutes of the earliest such event.

**Return:** `package_id`, `event_type`, `warehouse_id`, `copies`, `spread_minutes` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 2362 rows on the visible data):

| package_id | event_type | warehouse_id | copies | spread_minutes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | warehouse_departure | 4 | 2 | 11 |
| 3 | picked_up | 3 | 2 | 12 |
| 6 | warehouse_arrival | 22 | 2 | 13 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH s AS (SELECT package_id, event_type, warehouse_id, event_at, MIN(event_at) OVER (PARTITION BY package_id, event_type, warehouse_id) AS first_at FROM tracking_events WHERE event_source = 'scanner') SELECT package_id, event_type, warehouse_id, COUNT(*) AS copies, ROUND((julianday(MAX(event_at)) - julianday(first_at)) * 1440, 0) AS spread_minutes FROM s WHERE (julianday(event_at) - julianday(first_at)) * 1440 <= 15 GROUP BY package_id, event_type, warehouse_id, first_at HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
```

**Why it works.** Only copies close to the first scan are retries; a later scan at the same hub is a different event.

**Hints:** (1) Find the earliest event_at per group with MIN() OVER. (2) Keep rows within 15 minutes of it, then group and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Treats every repeat at the same hub as a retry, whatever the time gap.

### qb-0056 · Sessionize retries and exact boundaries

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Deduplicate, mark boundaries with a strict comparison, count per day. (rubric: Hard, score 9)
- **Topic:** Sessions & sequences (`dates.sessions`); tags `cleaning.dedupe`
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables events · read-only
- **Objective:** Build sessions with a precise inactivity rule.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 48 (Sessionize an event stream)

**Task.** For logical events (one per event_id) that occurred in June 2025, return session_date and sessions per UTC day. A user’s session starts at their first June event or after a gap strictly greater than 30 minutes; a session belongs to the date of its first event.

**Return:** `session_date`, `sessions` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 30 rows on the visible data):

| session_date | sessions |
| --- | --- |
| 2025-06-01 | 159 |
| 2025-06-02 | 200 |
| 2025-06-03 | 165 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH e AS (SELECT user_id, event_id, occurred_at FROM (SELECT * FROM (SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY received_at, delivery_id) AS copy FROM events e WHERE occurred_at >= '2025-06-01' AND occurred_at < '2025-07-01') WHERE copy = 1)), m AS (SELECT occurred_at, LAG(occurred_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) AS prev FROM e) SELECT date(occurred_at) AS session_date, COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM m WHERE prev IS NULL OR unixepoch(occurred_at) - unixepoch(prev) > 1800 GROUP BY session_date
```

**Why it works.** Counting session starts gives sessions; each session is credited to the day it began.

**Hints:** (1) Gap in seconds: unixepoch(occurred_at) − unixepoch(previous). (2) Count session starts per date(occurred_at).



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Starts a session at a gap of exactly 30 minutes.

### qb-0057 · Paid conversion by acquisition channel

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Conversion within a window from signup, by segment. (rubric: Medium, score 4.5)
- **Topic:** Funnels & conversion (`analytics.conversion`); tags `analytics.segmentation`
- **Dataset:** Product / SaaS Analytics · tables accounts, subscriptions · read-only
- **Objective:** Compare conversion rates across segments with a fixed window.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 52 (Experiment conversion denominators)

**Task.** For workspaces created before 2025-06-01, return acquisition_channel, workspaces, converted (workspaces with a paid subscription starting within 30 days of creation) and conversion_pct (0–100, 2 decimals).

**Return:** `acquisition_channel`, `workspaces`, `converted`, `conversion_pct` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 6 rows on the visible data):

| acquisition_channel | workspaces | converted | conversion_pct |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| organic | 948 | 61 | 6.43 |
| outbound_sales | 226 | 17 | 7.52 |
| paid_search | 700 | 57 | 8.14 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT acquisition_channel, COUNT(*) AS workspaces, SUM(converted) AS converted, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(converted) / COUNT(*), 2) AS conversion_pct FROM (SELECT a.acquisition_channel, EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM subscriptions s WHERE s.account_id = a.account_id AND s.plan <> 'free' AND s.started_at < datetime(a.created_at, '+30 days')) AS converted FROM accounts a WHERE a.created_at < '2025-06-01') GROUP BY acquisition_channel
```

**Why it works.** Every workspace is in the denominator; only upgrades within 30 days count.

### qb-0059 · Enforce delivery-slot rules

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Combine CHECK, UNIQUE and FOREIGN KEY constraints. (rubric: Medium, score 4)
- **Topic:** Constraints (`engineering.constraints`)
- **Dataset:** Logistics · tables warehouses · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Encode business rules as constraints.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 60 (Constraints protect the data contract)

**Task.** Create delivery_slots with slot_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, warehouse_id INTEGER NOT NULL referencing warehouses(warehouse_id), slot_date TEXT NOT NULL that must be a valid YYYY-MM-DD date, capacity INTEGER NOT NULL between 1 and 500, and at most one slot per warehouse and date. Insert (1, 1, '2025-05-01', 120) and (2, 1, '2025-05-02', 80). Return slot_id, warehouse_id, slot_date and capacity.

**Return:** `slot_id`, `warehouse_id`, `slot_date`, `capacity` · any row order

**Example output** (first 2 of 2 rows on the visible data):

| slot_id | warehouse_id | slot_date | capacity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 2025-05-01 | 120 |
| 2 | 1 | 2025-05-02 | 80 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
CREATE TABLE delivery_slots (slot_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, warehouse_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES warehouses(warehouse_id), slot_date TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (date(slot_date) = slot_date), capacity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (capacity BETWEEN 1 AND 500), UNIQUE (warehouse_id, slot_date)); INSERT INTO delivery_slots VALUES (1, 1, '2025-05-01', 120), (2, 1, '2025-05-02', 80); SELECT slot_id, warehouse_id, slot_date, capacity FROM delivery_slots
```

**Why it works.** Each rule is enforced on every write, not only checked in reports.

**Hints:** (1) CHECK (date(slot_date) = slot_date). (2) UNIQUE (warehouse_id, slot_date).



**Object checks:** 5 (write must fail, write must fail, write must fail, write must fail, valid write must succeed)

- Accepts impossible dates such as 2025-02-30.

### qb-0060 · Recover a partially failed transfer

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Savepoint recovery inside a transaction with state checks. (rubric: Easy, score 2)
- **Topic:** Transactions (`engineering.transactions`)
- **Dataset:** Finance / Payments · tables transactions · write-enabled lab
- **Objective:** Undo only the failed part of a unit of work.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 61 (Transactions & savepoint recovery)

**Task.** In one transaction: post a transfer_out of −25000 cents on account 1 and a matching transfer_in of 25000 on account 3 (both posted at '2025-06-30 12:00:00'); set a savepoint; post a 'fee' of −500 cents on account 1; roll back to the savepoint (the fee was charged in error); commit. Return transaction_type, account_id and amount_cents for ledger entries posted at '2025-06-30 12:00:00'.

**Return:** `transaction_type`, `account_id`, `amount_cents` · any row order

**Example output** (first 2 of 2 rows on the visible data):

| transaction_type | account_id | amount_cents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| transfer_out | 1 | -25000 |
| transfer_in | 3 | 25000 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
BEGIN; INSERT INTO transactions (account_id, transaction_type, status, amount_cents, initiated_at, posted_at, description) VALUES (1, 'transfer_out', 'posted', -25000, '2025-06-30 12:00:00', '2025-06-30 12:00:00', 'TRANSFER TO 3'), (3, 'transfer_in', 'posted', 25000, '2025-06-30 12:00:00', '2025-06-30 12:00:00', 'TRANSFER FROM 1'); SAVEPOINT fee; INSERT INTO transactions (account_id, transaction_type, status, amount_cents, initiated_at, posted_at, description) VALUES (1, 'fee', 'posted', -500, '2025-06-30 12:00:00', '2025-06-30 12:00:00', 'TRANSFER FEE'); ROLLBACK TO fee; COMMIT; SELECT transaction_type, account_id, amount_cents FROM transactions WHERE posted_at = '2025-06-30 12:00:00'
```

**Why it works.** ROLLBACK TO removes only the fee; COMMIT keeps both sides of the transfer.

**Hints:** (1) INSERT INTO transactions (account_id, transaction_type, status, amount_cents, initiated_at, posted_at, description) VALUES … (2) SAVEPOINT fee; …; ROLLBACK TO fee; COMMIT.

**Database-state checks:** 1 full query results compared with an independent reference database.

**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- RELEASE keeps the erroneous fee.

### qb-0061 · Products bought together

- **Difficulty:** Medium — Self-join on invoice with pair ordering and a count threshold. (rubric: Medium, score 5)
- **Topic:** Self joins (`joins.self`)
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items · read-only
- **Objective:** Count unordered pairs that occur together.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 34 (Self-joins & referral relationships)

**Task.** For sale orders in December 2011, return product_a, product_b (stock codes with product_a < product_b) and orders: the number of distinct orders containing both, for pairs bought together on at least 5 orders.

**Return:** `product_a`, `product_b`, `orders` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 10 rows on the visible data):

| product_a | product_b | orders |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 21914 | 23493 | 5 |
| 22086 | 22909 | 6 |
| 22086 | 22910 | 8 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
SELECT a.stock_code AS product_a, b.stock_code AS product_b, COUNT(DISTINCT a.order_id) AS orders FROM order_items a JOIN order_items b ON b.order_id = a.order_id AND a.stock_code < b.stock_code JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = a.order_id WHERE o.order_type = 'sale' AND o.ordered_at >= '2011-12-01' GROUP BY a.stock_code, b.stock_code HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.order_id) >= 5
```

**Why it works.** a < b lists each pair once; distinct orders avoid counting repeated lines twice.

**Hints:** (1) Join order_items to itself on order_id with a.stock_code < b.stock_code. (2) COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) handles repeated lines.



**Rejected wrong approaches (tested):**
- Lists each pair twice and counts repeated lines.

### qb-0063 · Department audience overlap

- **Difficulty:** Hard — Reduce to customer-department pairs before self-joining. (rubric: Hard, score 6.25)
- **Topic:** Join fan-out & cardinality (`joins.fan-out`); tags `joins.self`
- **Dataset:** Retail · tables orders, order_items, products, categories · read-only
- **Objective:** Count shared members between groups without fan-out.
- **Prerequisite lessons:** 49 (Multi-grain joins without fan-out), 34 (Self-joins & referral relationships)

**Task.** For December 2011 sale orders by identified customers, return department_a, department_b (department_a < department_b) and shared_customers: customers who bought from both departments.

**Return:** `department_a`, `department_b`, `shared_customers` · any row order

**Example output** (first 3 of 28 rows on the visible data):

| department_a | department_b | shared_customers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fashion | Gifts | 44 |
| Fashion | Home | 45 |
| Fashion | Kids | 26 |

**Reference solution**

```sql
WITH cd AS (SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id, c.department FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id JOIN products p ON p.stock_code = i.stock_code JOIN categories c ON c.category_id = p.category_id WHERE o.order_type = 'sale' AND o.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND o.ordered_at >= '2011-12-01') SELECT a.department AS department_a, b.department AS department_b, COUNT(*) AS shared_customers FROM cd a JOIN cd b ON b.customer_id = a.customer_id AND a.department < b.department GROUP BY a.department, b.department
```

**Why it works.** Deduplicating to customer-department first means each customer counts once per pair.

**Hints:** (1) First SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, department. (2) Self-join that result on customer_id with a.department < b.department.

- Without DISTINCT, line counts multiply and inflate the overlap.
